newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil gov't cannot celebrate re-election yet.
newsitem.headline: Brazil gov't cannot celebrate re-election yet.

text.p: Brazil's government can barely afford to celebrate a key victory in President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's re-election plan, as the opposition seeks to alter the reform and a potentially destabilizing power battle looms.
"There weren't any wild celebrations last night because there's still a long way to go," said a government source in Congress.

Cardoso scored the biggest political victory of his two-year term on Tuesday night when the Chamber of Deputies approved a constitutional amendment that would let him run in the 1998 presidential elections.

The amendment, which would also allow state governors and mayors the chance of a second consecutive term, has yet to be approved in a second vote on the floor of the lower house and then moves on the Senate.
Political commentators said the government's hard-fought victory might prove costly in terms of bad feeling within normally allied parties.

"Today...is a like day we have all seen in the films -- some soldiers wandering about in a completely destroyed field and still smoke rising here and there," wrote columnist Fernando Rodrigues in newspaper Folha de Sao Paulo.

The government's top priority would be to defeat a series of opposition amendments to the re-election bill, including a proposal for a referendum on the issue and another forcing Cardoso to step down for six months before seeking re-election.
The Chamber of Deputies had been due to begin voting on the amendments on Wednesday morning but the process appeared to have been delayed until the afternoon.
The next challenge for the government would be to guarantee victory for its candidate in next week's election for a new president of the Chamber of Deputies.

The government supports Michel Temer, lower house leader of the powerful Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB), who played a key role in Tuesday's victory by persuading nearly half the party's 102 deputies to vote with the government.

The PMDB had threatened to derail Cardoso's re-election drive and its members could still vote against re-election when it is put to its second lower house vote around February 15 if Temer is defeated in next week's elections.
"If he loses and the PMDB thinks the government had a hand in it then we could be in trouble," said the government source.

There is the risk of even more fallout in the normally sedate Senate where influential PMDB senators were reported to be furious the government had ignore their demands that an election to choose a new president there had to come before any vote on re-election.
"There's a lot of bad blood," said a PMDB official in the Senate. "Cardoso can't take re-election for granted here."

Re-election might also face a rough ride in the upper house because many senators are believed to have their eye on running for governor in 1998 and may want to rewrite the bill to deny current holders of those offices the chance of running again.
If changed in the upper house, the bill would have to go back to the Chamber of Deputies.
